hooks: What goes into a cocoa protein bar besides the protein?
angles.idea: Carousel — A cocoa bar explained by its actual recipe
angles.usefulInsight: Content job: turn ingredient transparency into product understanding rather than another instruction to read labels. Awareness hypothesis: the reader knows protein bars but does not know this brand or what goes into its Double Cocoa variant. Opening/payoff pair: ask what makes a cocoa protein bar beyond the protein number; deliver the specific declared combination of cocoa powder, cocoa butter, dates, cashews, almonds and whey. The ingredient names are visible together on the Double Cocoa wrapper in image-5; do not extrapolate quantities, texture, sweetness levels or nutritional superiority. Intended progression: establish the buying question, unpack the cocoa pair, reveal the rest of the declared recipe, then connect this concrete example to the brand's upfront-disclosure belief and invite exploration. Supported mechanism: an actual front-of-pack ingredient declaration, grounded in the brand statement E72. Framework: feature → practical distinction → reader value, with the value being a more concrete picture of the product. Image relationship: image-5 is direct product evidence, specifically its upper wrapper; it is not an unwrapped-food demonstration. Comparison: high reader recognition, strong specific discovery, high credibility within the limits of the wrapper, and strong brand fit.

hooks: Cocoa, peanut or coffee? Your 20g protein bar has options.
angles.idea: Static — Choose the flavour, keep the 20g
angles.usefulInsight: Content job: create a direct, flavour-led reason to browse the Pro bar range, separate from the carousel's ingredient education. Awareness hypothesis: the reader already wants a protein bar and would welcome a choice beyond a single cocoa flavour. Opening/payoff pair: frame cocoa, peanut or coffee as the immediate appetite decision; show that the three photographed Pro wrappers each declare 20g protein. Supported mechanism: image-5 visibly names Double Cocoa, Peanut Cocoa and Coffee Cocoa and carries the same 20g declaration on each. That supports a shared protein amount, not otherwise identical nutrition, equal serving weights or equivalent effects. Framework: desire-led AIDA, compressed into one complete buying idea: three flavour directions with a common declared protein amount, followed by an invitation to explore the range. Image relationship: image-5 supplies both product presence and the relevant variant evidence. Comparison: strongest immediate reader recognition and image fit, moderate discovery, high specificity and credibility, and strong commercial fit.

hooks: Does your snack need to look picture-perfect?
angles.idea: Alternative — Packaged food need not look picture-perfect
angles.usefulInsight: Content job: introduce the brand's unusual willingness to acknowledge imperfect appearance. Awareness hypothesis: some shoppers expect packaged snacks to match polished food photography. Opening/payoff pair: question whether visual perfection should be the expectation; explain the brand's own admission that its food does not always look perfect. Framework: belief → distinction → example → action. Supported mechanism is limited to the brand-authored admission, not a demonstrated relationship between appearance and ingredients. Image relationship: no supplied asset clearly documents a real imperfect product; image-3 is highly styled and cannot serve as that proof. Comparison: distinctive discovery and strong voice fit, but weaker buying relevance and substantially weaker visual credibility than the selected ideas. Do not imply that irregular appearance proves safety, naturalness or nutritional quality.

strategy.imageStyle: Inspected raster assets: image-0 shows two hollow, four-point sparkle shapes in muted berry pink, arranged diagonally against a black-displayed background; decorative, not product evidence. image-1 shows two overlapping upright white-and-green plant-protein pouches, with the rear pouch higher and left. Burgundy and beige flavour panels distinguish them; large green lettering dominates their fronts. No setting or people are visible. image-2 is a wide lavender-and-purple studio banner: two upright food-drink pouches and small glasses of brown liquid sit centrally on a purple surface, with blue headline text above and a white pill-shaped button below. image-3 is a wide hot-pink banner, with pale headline text and a button on the left; on the right, a wrapped bar sits behind a mound of golden-brown nut pieces while a dark glossy stream descends onto the product arrangement. This is styled advertising imagery, not evidence of a manufacturing process. image-5 shows three horizontally wrapped bars stacked vertically against a black-displayed background: burgundy Double Cocoa, orange Peanut Cocoa and brown Coffee Cocoa. Each wrapper has a prominent white triangular panel marked 20g protein, white brand lettering and smaller ingredient text. No people or consumption setting are shown. diagram-0 was supplied only as SVG metadata and was not visually inspected. Retain the site's condensed sans-serif character and berry, pink, white and dark-ink vocabulary; these assets are source material, not finished designs.
strategy.market: Consumer packaged foods, with these posts focused on protein bars. Selling geography, buyer demographics, company stage, social following and customer count are unknown.
strategy.mechanism: Make the brand's ingredient-disclosure belief concrete through the visible Double Cocoa Protein Bars Pro wrapper, then use the three photographed Pro variants for a separate flavour-led buying idea. Packaging demonstrates what the brand declares, not health outcomes or customer satisfaction.
strategy.note: The selected carousel wins on concrete recipe discovery: it demonstrates the brand's disclosure belief instead of merely telling shoppers to inspect ingredients. The static wins on immediate appetite relevance and a complete product-backed buying proposition. They perform different jobs—understanding one recipe versus choosing among flavour directions—even though the same supplied product asset supports both. Proposed carousel family: annotation, reference S008-01, because an actual wrapper anchors the explanation. Proposed static family: hero, reference S008-04, because the three-bar asset directly carries the offer. These are conceptual family selections, not slide copy or design specifications; reference screenshots were not inspected. Preserve readable evidence rather than enlarging claims from tiny packaging text. Exact source anchors include E2: "We're a clean-label food brand"; E10: "Protein Bars Pro"; and E72: "Our purpose is simple. We make food so clean, we can proudly declare every single ingredient that goes into it, upfront. And we can speak the whole truth, because we have #nothingtohide." Use only the protein-amount portion supported by E11 and the visible wrappers; do not repeat its broad 'No chemicals' language. Homepage offers address different needs: powders and plant protein, portable bars, cocoa snacks and food education. The story page supports the disclosure belief; the sparse Hazelnut Millet page supplies no recipe evidence for these posts. The True Story page is not a campaign topic, and contested sugar claims are excluded. Motivations, awareness and the shopping occasion remain creative hypotheses. Current stock, prices and variant availability are unverified, so avoid urgency and purchase guarantees. No supplied reviews, customer messages, before/after evidence or process photographs support testimonial, transformation or manufacturing-demonstration formats. Do not use the existing styled banner as proof of taste or texture. Both posts have one next action: explore the Pro range from the inspected homepage. Any Instagram profile-link wording depends on the manual publishing setup.

blocks.text: We Believe Good Food is Made of Good Ingredients. So, Our Products Contains Natural Ingredients that are Mentioned on them and Nothing Else.
Ever wondered why most brands hide their ingredient list, in microscopic font, at the back? Why you’re made to stare, squint eyed, at the crimp, just to figure out what your food is made of?
As an obese kid trying to eat healthy, I used to ask these questions everyday. I never got an answer, so I did my own research.
Brands hide what goes into their food, because they have something to hide.

Because they’d rather have you drool over fake pictures of molten, drippy chocolate, than have you discover that your food contains artificial sugars and preservatives and other hard-to-pronounce chemicals.
In the name of ‘healthy’, we’re being sold a bunch of lies. And I was done being lied to. So I, along with a few like-minded (and equally betrayed) folks, started The Whole Truth.
Our purpose is simple. We make food so clean, we can proudly declare every single ingredient that goes into it, upfront. And we can speak the whole truth, because we have #nothingtohide.
ShashankFounder. CEO. Obese kid. Fit adult. Hell bent on setting packaged food right.
Who is this guy?

Shashank, our main man, started his fitness journey at over 100kgs, 15 years ago. In the decade that followed, he taught himself fitness, lost 40kgs, ran several marathons, and helped many friends and colleagues get onto the fitness bandwagon.
After all the years of research and self-experimentation, he believes there’s only one universal food truth
good food is made of good ingredients
You can access all his learnings at FITSHIT.in, his free-forever fitness blog read by thousands every week.
Disclaimer – views on the blog are personal. so is the crusade.
PS: It is very strange to write about yourself in third person.

writerRun.review: buyer-value-v2: The posts stay within the supplied product evidence: Double Cocoa’s declared six ingredients, the three photographed Pro variants and their shared 20g protein declaration. Nuts and whey support the plant-only distinction without implying health benefits or nutritional superiority. The homepage is an appropriate destination for exploring Protein Bars Pro; the unrelated Hazelnut Millet page is not used as proof. Both formats give unfamiliar protein-bar shoppers a concrete buying idea: the carousel reveals the cocoa-and-nut combination behind the Double Cocoa name, while the static makes flavour choice compatible with a shared protein amount. The carousel progresses from appetite to recipe, suitability, disclosure rationale and action, although its ingredient-preference slide is the weakest editorial beat. The static performs a complementary discovery job rather than repeating the recipe explanation. Product assets, observed colours and brand-authored language are consistent with the supplied evidence, with no invented testimonials, outcomes or availability claims.
